questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, is in ED with sudden left leg weakness and numbness. You have established he was last known well at 09:30 today and that he takes apixaban, which he often forgets. A code stroke has been called. Which further history item most directly decides whether he can have thrombolysis?
options: Whether he has had similar brief episodes of leg weakness before
When he last ate or drank anything by mouth
The exact time and date of his last apixaban dose
Whether he smokes or uses recreational drugs such as cocaine
questions.why: A DOAC taken in the last 48 hours rules out thrombolysis unless a drug-specific level shows no relevant effect. So the timing of the last dose, together with the last known well time, must be pinned down early.
notes: His earlier TIAs matter for the diagnosis and for urgent secondary prevention, but they do not decide whether he can be thrombolysed.
He must stay nil by mouth until a swallow screen, but the time of his last meal has no bearing on reperfusion eligibility.
Smoking and cocaine are risk factors to deal with in secondary prevention, but neither stops him having thrombolysis.

questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, has a right A2 occlusion and no haemorrhage on CT. Onset was 09:30 and it is now 12:00. His last apixaban dose was at 7 pm last night. INR 1.1, APTT 33 s, platelets 236. An apixaban-calibrated anti-Xa level is pending. Which statement best guides the decision on thrombolysis?
options: Thrombolyse now, as the normal INR and APTT show no significant residual apixaban effect
Withhold thrombolysis unless the apixaban anti-Xa level shows no relevant drug effect
Give idarucizumab to reverse the apixaban, then proceed with thrombolysis
Thrombolyse now, because more than 12 hours have passed since his last apixaban dose
questions.why: Apixaban taken within 48 hours contraindicates thrombolysis unless a drug-calibrated anti-Xa level shows no relevant effect under the local protocol. A normal INR and APTT do not exclude a clinically important apixaban effect.
notes: INR and APTT are not reliable for apixaban, so normal values do not show that the drug has cleared.
Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran only. Reversing a DOAC just so you can thrombolyse is not standard practice.
The usual cut-off is 48 hours unless a drug-specific level is reassuring. Seventeen hours after the last dose, he may still have a meaningful anticoagulant effect.

questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, has an acute right anterior cerebral artery stroke. He has wet himself twice without warning since onset. He can pass urine normally, the bladder scan shows no retention, and saddle sensation is intact. Which mechanism best explains his incontinence?
options: Detrusor areflexia with overflow from loss of sacral parasympathetic supply
Detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia from interruption of the suprasacral spinal cord pathways
Urethral sphincter weakness from loss of pudendal nerve motor supply
Loss of cortical inhibition of the pontine micturition centre (uninhibited detrusor)
questions.why: The medial frontal and paracentral cortex, supplied by the ACA, normally keeps the pontine micturition centre in check. When this is lost, the bladder empties in full, coordinated contractions without warning, and there is no retention.
notes: An areflexic bladder overflows with a large residual volume, as in cauda equina syndrome, but his bladder scan shows no retention.
Dyssynergia comes from a spinal cord lesion between the pons and the sacral cord and causes incomplete emptying. His lesion is cortical, so the pontine coordination of voiding still works.
Pudendal nerve damage causes stress incontinence, usually with saddle sensory loss. His saddle sensation is intact.

questions.stem: Mr Rodriguez, 65, has a CT angiogram showing abrupt occlusion of the right anterior cerebral artery in the proximal A2 segment. Isolated ACA territory infarcts are uncommon, about 2% of ischaemic strokes. Why does an A2 occlusion cause infarction when an A1 occlusion is often tolerated?
options: A2 lies distal to the anterior communicating artery, so the other ACA cannot cross-fill
A2 lies distal to the posterior communicating artery, so PCA inflow cannot reach the A2
A2 gives off the lenticulostriate arteries, which are end arteries without collaterals
A2 has no leptomeningeal anastomoses with MCA branches, unlike the A1 segment
questions.why: The anterior communicating artery joins the two A1–A2 junctions. If A1 is blocked, the other ACA can still fill the distal territory, but a blockage beyond ACom (A2) loses this protection, so the paracentral lobule infarcts.
notes: The posterior communicating artery joins the internal carotid artery to the PCA. It is not part of the ACA's route of supply.
The lenticulostriate arteries come mainly from the M1 segment of the MCA and supply deep structures, not the medial cortex where the leg is represented.
The distal ACA cortical branches do have leptomeningeal anastomoses with the MCA and PCA. That is part of why he has salvageable penumbra on perfusion imaging.
